architectural_implications.after: Agents are portable packages defined in code and executed by any conforming runtime, with runtime responsibilities separated from agent responsibilities.
architectural_implications.before: Every team hand-builds its own orchestration loop, retry logic, tool dispatch, and state handling, producing agents that cannot be shared or composed.
architectural_implications.consequence: Distribution and composition become possible, but the spec and runtime contract become a new critical dependency that must be versioned and governed.
architectural_implications.observation: The harness stops being bespoke per-company code and becomes a spec-conformant package executed by a runtime.

architectural_implications.after: Each narrow agent pins its own model, potentially a smaller cheaper one, chosen for that job.
architectural_implications.before: An organization picks one frontier model for all AI features and layers skills/tools on top of it.
architectural_implications.consequence: Cost and latency can drop sharply, but fleet management now involves many pinned models with different upgrade and deprecation timelines.
architectural_implications.observation: Model selection moves from a platform-wide decision to a per-agent property.

architectural_implications.after: A coding agent reads the process PDF and emits a complete agent package with tools, prompts, threads, and endpoints in minutes.
architectural_implications.before: A process document is read by humans who then hand-write prompts, tool schemas, and glue code.
architectural_implications.consequence: Throughput of agent creation rises, but review of generated definitions (tool scope, prompt correctness) becomes the new bottleneck and the main safety control.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent construction becomes a code-generation pipeline fed by business process documents.

architectural_implications.after: The runtime surfaces tool calls, token usage, cost, and cache rate uniformly for any conforming agent.
architectural_implications.before: Each custom harness logs whatever it happens to log; cost and cache behavior are invisible or inconsistent.
architectural_implications.consequence: Cross-agent cost and reliability comparisons become feasible, enabling portfolio-level decisions about which agents to keep, downgrade, or retune.
architectural_implications.observation: Observability is treated as a runtime contract property rather than something each agent implements.

article_ideas.angle: Layer-by-layer standards analysis showing where lock-in actually lives and why the empty harness slot blocks distribution.
article_ideas.based_on: The harness — the orchestration layer that turns a model into an agent — is the one layer of the agent stack with no standard
article_ideas.thesis: Tool, prompt, and transport standards are converging, but the orchestration harness remains the unstandardized layer that determines whether agents can be packaged, evaluated, and composed; standardizing it is higher leverage than adding more model capability.
article_ideas.title: The Missing Layer: Why the Harness Is the Real Agent Interoperability Battle

article_ideas.angle: Architecture argument with cost, evaluation, and composition tradeoffs.
article_ideas.based_on: Decompose at the job boundary, not the skill boundary
article_ideas.thesis: Capability breadth is a liability, not a feature; decomposing at the job boundary into single-job agents on small pinned models beats a frontier model with dozens of skills on cost, evaluability, and composability—provided orchestration quality keeps up.
article_ideas.title: Stop Building One Agent With All the Tools

article_ideas.angle: Mental-model shift and its consequences for CI, testing, and code review.
article_ideas.based_on: an agent is deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic model output
article_ideas.thesis: Reliable agents come from a deterministic TypeScript shell—typed tools, hooks, effects, threads—around an unreliable model, not from better prompting; this relocates reliability engineering into testable code and makes agents reviewable like software.

article_ideas.angle: Resolve the apparent contradiction in the specification's five principles and derive operational rules.

article_ideas.based_on: agents are vendor-agnostic and portable at the runtime layer, but each agent is coupled to a specific model
article_ideas.thesis: The agent portability debate conflates two axes: runtime and package portability versus behavioral repeatability. The workable architecture is vendor-agnostic packaging with per-agent model pinning; teams that chase model-agnostic behavior lose evaluation stability.
article_ideas.title: Pin the Model, Port the Runtime

connections.relationship: Complementary stack layers: the spec occupies the orchestration slot left empty by standards for tools, prompts, and transport.
Pinning a model per agent is the precondition for stable, comparable per-agent evaluation; an unpinned model makes regression results non-reproducible.
Narrow agents with per-agent token, cost, and cache-rate telemetry make cost per business task measurable, which is impractical in a monolithic general agent.
A typed, declarative artifact is what makes the package generatable and reviewable by a coding agent from a process document.
Scoping tools per agent mirrors credential scoping per service; the agent's tool surface is the enforcement boundary.

evidence_quotes.text: Existing standards cover tool access (MCP), prompts (Skills, Agents.md), and communication (A2A, ACP, payments), but nothing exists for the harness itself.
Agents are hard because building an agent means building a harness with dozens of complex orchestration requirements.

core_insights.generalization: Standards emerge bottom-up by layer; whichever layer is left unstandardized becomes the source of fragmentation and vendor lock-in for everything above it.
core_insights.insight: The harness — the orchestration layer that turns a model into an agent — is the one layer of the agent stack with no standard, while tool access (MCP), prompt/skill packaging (Skills, Agents.md), and inter-agent communication (A2A, ACP, payments) are all already standardized. This makes the harness the highest-leverage place for a new specification.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It tells engineers exactly where the interoperability gap lives and where to invest abstraction effort: not in tools, prompts, or transport, but in the orchestration contract that binds model, prompt, tools, state, and runtime together.

evidence_quotes.text: A Gmail agent beats a Gmail skill because a single-job agent is cheaper, easier to evaluate, and composes into larger systems.
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash configured as a dedicated Gmail agent is cheaper, more evaluable, and easier to compose than Claude Opus with 41 skills.

core_insights.generalization: Capability should be allocated at the smallest independently evaluable unit; composition replaces configuration breadth.
core_insights.insight: Decompose at the job boundary, not the skill boundary: a dedicated single-job agent on a small cheap model is claimed to be cheaper, easier to evaluate, and composable into larger systems, versus one frontier model loaded with dozens of tools and skills.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It is a concrete architectural rule for where to cut agent boundaries, and it flips the default instinct of adding capabilities to one general agent. It also implies evaluation surfaces are per-agent, which changes how CI, benchmarks, and cost accounting are structured.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents are deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective.
Everything is code written in TypeScript for file-based definitions, typed references, hooks, effects, threads, and runtimes.

core_insights.generalization: Treat the model as an unreliable dependency behind a deterministic boundary; push every decision that can be decided in code out of the model.
core_insights.insight: The spec's framing is that an agent is deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic model output — which relocates control flow, tool invocation, hooks, and effects into ordinary code, leaving the model as a constrained component rather than the system itself.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This framing determines where reliability engineering happens: in typed, testable code paths around the model rather than in prompt engineering. It also makes the agent testable like software (deterministic shell, stubbed model) rather than only evaluable end-to-end.

evidence_quotes.text: If an agent can do anything, it might do anything, which is an unacceptable liability.
Domain-specific agents must have strictly restricted, fine-tuned scopes and workflows.

core_insights.generalization: Least-privilege applies to agent tool surfaces exactly as it does to service credentials; instruction-level constraints are not an enforcement mechanism.
core_insights.insight: Capability breadth is a liability: an agent with unrestricted tool access may take unintended actions, so trust is achieved by strictly scoping tools and workflow rather than by instructing a general model to stay on task.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It converts a vague 'safety' concern into a concrete design constraint — the tool surface and workflow graph are the enforcement boundary, not the system prompt. This directly affects permission models, allowlists, and blast-radius design.

evidence_quotes.text: Claude Code reads a warranty process PDF and builds a complete standard agent package in minutes.
Generated code includes explicit tools, pinned models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), system prompts, threads, and HTTP endpoints.

core_insights.generalization: Any domain artifact that becomes a typed, file-based spec immediately becomes automatable by coding agents and reviewable by normal engineering process.
core_insights.insight: A file-based, TypeScript-typed agent definition (models, prompts, agents, threads, HTTP endpoints) becomes a build artifact that a coding agent can generate from a process document — turning agent construction into a compile target rather than hand-written glue.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If the agent package is a declarative artifact, generation, review, diffing, and deployment all become standard software supply-chain operations. It implies agent definition files should be treated like source code with review gates, not like prompts stored in a database.

evidence_quotes.text: Five core principles: vendor-agnostic, domain-specific, coupled to a model, composable, and portable.
Generated code includes explicit tools, pinned models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), system prompts, threads, and HTTP endpoints.

core_insights.generalization: Vary what must be portable (packaging, runtime contract) and pin what must be reproducible (model version, weights, temperature); the two are different axes, not a single 'agnostic vs locked' choice.
core_insights.insight: The spec deliberately holds two opposing positions at once: agents are vendor-agnostic and portable at the runtime layer, but each agent is coupled to a specific model. Portability lives in the definition format; repeatability lives in the pinned model.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This resolves a common confusion in agent architecture — teams conflate 'model agnosticism' with 'deterministic behavior'. Pinning the model per agent while keeping the runtime swappable is what makes evaluation meaningful without sacrificing deployment flexibility.

document.description: One-paragraph summary of Every Company Is Building Agents That Can't Work Together - Justin Schroeder, Standard Agents

key_claims.claim: Existing agent standards cover tool access, prompt packaging, and inter-agent communication, but no standard exists for the harness itself.
key_claims.evidence: Existing standards cover tool access (MCP), prompts (Skills, Agents.md), and communication (A2A, ACP, payments), but nothing exists for the harness itself.
key_claims.verification_question: Do any existing specifications define the harness/orchestration contract (state, hooks, effects, runtime boundary) rather than tools, prompts, or transport?

key_claims.claim: A dedicated single-job agent on a small model outperforms a broad frontier model configured with many tools and skills on cost, evaluability, and composability.
key_claims.evidence: A Gmail agent beats a Gmail skill because a single-job agent is cheaper, easier to evaluate, and composes into larger systems.
key_claims.verification_question: On matched tasks, what are the success rate, cost per task, and latency for a small-model single-job agent versus a frontier model with equivalent skills?

key_claims.claim: Unconstrained agents are a liability because broad capability implies the possibility of unauthorized action.
key_claims.evidence: If an agent can do anything, it might do anything, which is an unacceptable liability.
key_claims.verification_question: Under what tool-surface breadth does observed out-of-scope action rate rise materially, and does prompt-level instruction reduce it measurably?

key_claims.claim: An agent should be defined as deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic model output toward a defined objective.
key_claims.evidence: Agents are deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective.

key_claims.claim: Business value derives from operational processes, so agents must integrate into those processes rather than act as generic standalone assistants.
key_claims.evidence: A business is its processes; everything valuable comes from well-functioning processes.
key_claims.verification_question: Do agent deployments that integrate into a defined process show higher retention or business-metric impact than general-purpose assistant deployments in the same organization?

key_claims.claim: A coding agent can generate a complete, runnable agent package (tools, pinned model, prompts, threads, HTTP endpoints) from a process PDF in minutes.
key_claims.evidence: Claude Code reads a warranty process PDF and builds a complete standard agent package in minutes.
key_claims.verification_question: Reproducing the demo on held-out process documents, what fraction of generated agent packages run successfully without manual edits, and what classes of errors dominate?

key_claims.claim: The specification defines five principles: vendor-agnostic, domain-specific, coupled to a model, composable, and portable.
key_claims.evidence: Five core principles: vendor-agnostic, domain-specific, coupled to a model, composable, and portable.
key_claims.verification_question: Are all five principles independently checkable in a conforming implementation, or do some (portability, composability) lack a testable conformance criterion?

open_questions.question: Does a spec-level harness definition actually produce identical behavior across different runtimes, or does runtime-specific behavior leak through hooks, effects, and thread semantics?
open_questions.research_direction: Build a conformance test suite for the spec and run the same agent package on at least two independent runtimes, diffing tool-call traces and outputs.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary states portability as a principle and demonstrates execution only on the AgentBuilder runtime; no cross-runtime conformance evidence or test suite is described.

open_questions.question: Can a hierarchy of small single-job agents composed together match the end-to-end task success rate of one frontier model with many skills, or only beat it on cost and evaluability?
open_questions.research_direction: Benchmark identical end-to-end tasks under three configurations: frontier model with N skills, single-job small-model agents composed by an orchestrator, and a hybrid; measure success rate, cost per success, and latency.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary asserts the single-job agent is cheaper, more evaluable, and easier to compose, but provides no accuracy or success-rate comparison — cost and quality are separate axes.

open_questions.question: How does a composed graph of agents pinned to different model versions handle model deprecation, upgrade, and rollback without invalidating evaluations of the whole system?
open_questions.research_direction: Prototype an agent registry that records pinned model versions per agent, then measure how many downstream agents must be re-evaluated when one pinned model is deprecated.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary describes coupling each agent to a model and making agents composable, but says nothing about versioning, deprecation timelines, or how a model change propagates through a composed agent graph.

open_questions.question: Are trust constraints enforced by the spec (declared tool allowlists and workflow boundaries) or only by the runtime sandbox — and which one actually prevents an agent from taking an unauthorized action?
open_questions.research_direction: Red-team a generated agent package by injecting prompts that attempt out-of-scope tool calls, and observe whether enforcement happens at definition validation, runtime dispatch, or not at all.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary names trust as a core adoption factor and advocates restricted scopes, but does not describe an enforcement mechanism, permission model, or sandbox.

open_questions.question: What fraction of a real business process can be captured in a generated agent package from a process document before human decomposition into multiple agents becomes necessary?
open_questions.research_direction: Take one multi-process domain and measure generation quality and failure rate as the process document grows in scope and branching.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The demo covers a single warranty claim agent; the summary gives no data on how the approach scales to the multi-process operations (scheduling, permits, billing disputes) it cites as motivating examples.

project_ideas.based_on: Does a spec-level harness definition actually produce identical behavior across different runtimes
project_ideas.hypothesis: Two independent runtimes executing the same spec-conformant agent package will produce identical tool-call traces for deterministic test cases, with divergence confined to explicitly declared runtime hooks and effects.
project_ideas.measurement: Percentage of test cases with identical traces; divergence categorized by hook, effect, and thread semantics; count of runtime-specific leaks.
project_ideas.name: Harness Conformance Diff Lab
project_ideas.poc: Implement a small agent package with one job, three tools, one hook, and one effect; run it on a reference runtime and an independent stub runtime; capture normalized tool-call and state traces for a fixed test suite; diff the traces.

project_ideas.based_on: Are trust constraints enforced by the spec (declared tool allowlists and workflow boundaries) or only by the runtime sandbox
project_ideas.hypothesis: Definition-level tool allowlists and workflow boundaries block out-of-scope tool invocations at 95% or more, while prompt-only instructions block less than 50% under adversarial prompts.
project_ideas.measurement: Out-of-scope attempt success rate per variant; enforcement layer that blocked each attempt; false-positive rate on legitimate tasks.
project_ideas.name: Agent Scope Red-Team Gate
project_ideas.poc: Generate a narrow warranty-claim agent package, then create three variants: spec allowlist, runtime sandbox only, and prompt-only. Run a prompt-injection suite attempting unauthorized billing and scheduling tool calls, and log the enforcement point and outcome.

project_ideas.based_on: Can a hierarchy of small single-job agents composed together match the end-to-end task success rate
project_ideas.hypothesis: A composed set of single-job small-model agents achieves at least 90% of a frontier model's end-to-end task success rate at 40% or less cost per successful task on a multi-step business workflow.
project_ideas.measurement: Task success rate, cost per success, p95 latency, and failure taxonomy; identify steps where composition loses accuracy.
project_ideas.name: Small-Agent Composition Benchmark
project_ideas.poc: Implement a four-step workflow—intake, lookup, decision, response—in two configurations: one frontier model with all skills and tools, and four single-job agents on small pinned models orchestrated by code. Use synthetic and replayed cases.

project_ideas.based_on: How does a composed graph of agents pinned to different model versions handle model deprecation
project_ideas.hypothesis: A dependency-aware agent registry that records per-agent pinned model versions and composition edges reduces the re-evaluation set for a single model deprecation from all agents to only direct and transitive dependents, cutting re-evaluations by 60% or more in a 20-agent graph.
project_ideas.measurement: Number of agents re-evaluated; false negatives where affected agents are not flagged; time to produce an upgrade plan.
project_ideas.name: Pinned-Model Deprecation Registry
project_ideas.poc: Build a registry manifest for 20 agents across five pinned models with composition edges; simulate deprecating one model; compute naive re-evaluation versus graph-scoped re-evaluation; prototype rollback and upgrade propagation.

source.title: Every Company Is Building Agents That Can't Work Together - Justin Schroeder, Standard Agents

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Justin Schroeder
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Standardizing AI Agents via the Standard Agent Specification
  • Purpose: To introduce and open-source the Standard Agent Specification and Standard Agent Builder, establishing an open ecosystem of interoperable, domain-specific agents. Justin Schroeder introduces the Standard Agent Specification, an open-source, engineering-first approach to building, packaging, and running domain-specific AI agents. He highlights why prevailing approaches—such as combining MCP servers and markdown files with general models—fail because businesses require control, reliability, repeatability, and non-generic tone. The talk details the three primary factors for agent adoption (Integration, Trust, Efficacy) and outlines the core specification principles: agents must be vendor-agnostic, domain-specific, coupled to a model, composable, and portable, implemented in TypeScript via file-based definitions, threads, hooks, effects, and runtimes.

Topic Map

The Observation: Everyone Is Building Agents

  • Explanation: An observation that while prevailing wisdom suggests building MCP servers and markdown documentation for smart general models (like Grok or Claude), businesses continue building custom agents because of deeper needs.
  • Key claims:
    • Everyone is building agents to power their business.
    • Prevailing wisdom says to build MCP servers and markdown files for smart general agents, but companies still build custom agents.
  • Examples:
    • Grok bot or Claude used with markdown files and MCP servers.
  • Terminology:
    • MCP servers
    • Agent MD
    • Smart general agent
  • Why it matters: Highlights the gap between general-purpose AI development and actual enterprise operational requirements.

The Three Factors: Integration, Trust, Efficacy

  • Explanation: Explains why people build custom agents based on three primary factors: deep business process integration, strict trust (doing what it was told and nothing else), and efficacy (doing the task well).
  • Key claims:
    • A business is its processes; everything valuable comes from well-functioning processes.
    • If an agent can do anything, it might do anything, which is an unacceptable liability.
    • Efficacy is about whether an agent can do the task and improve business performance.
  • Examples:
    • HVAC repair shop managing warranty claims, crew scheduling, and permits.
    • University managing financial aid and admissions.
    • Cloud provider managing incident response and billing disputes.
  • Terminology:
    • Integration
    • Trust
    • Efficacy
    • Liability
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates why businesses reject unconstrained general agents in favor of tightly scoped, dependable domain-specific workflows.

The Limits of Current Approaches & The Need for Standards

  • Explanation: Discusses why single-agent-does-everything approaches and ad-hoc custom harnesses fail to scale, lack distribution, and cannot be easily composed.
  • Key claims:
    • A Gmail agent beats a Gmail skill because a single-job agent is cheaper, easier to evaluate, and composes into larger systems.
    • Agents are hard because building an agent means building a harness with dozens of complex orchestration requirements.
    • Existing standards cover tool access (MCP), prompts (Skills, Agents.md), and communication (A2A, ACP, payments), but nothing exists for the harness itself.
  • Examples:
    • Claude Opus 5.5 with 112 tool definitions and 41 skills vs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash running a single-job Gmail agent.
  • Terminology:
    • The harness
    • MCP
    • Skills
    • A2A
    • ACP
    • Composability
  • Why it matters: Justifies the necessity of a standardized agent specification rather than fragmented, custom-built harnesses.

The Standard Agent Specification

  • Explanation: Introduces the Standard Agent Specification (standardagentspec.org) as an open-source, engineering-first approach where agents are deterministic software harnessing non-deterministic models.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents are deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective.
    • Five core principles: vendor-agnostic, domain-specific, coupled to a model, composable, and portable.
    • Everything is code written in TypeScript for file-based definitions, typed references, hooks, effects, threads, and runtimes.
  • Examples:
    • Defining models, prompts, and agents using defineModel, definePrompt, and defineAgent in TypeScript.
  • Terminology:
    • Standard Agent Specification
    • Deterministic software
    • Vendor-agnostic
    • TypeScript
    • Runtime contract
  • Why it matters: Provides a concrete engineering specification that solves speed, consistency, portability, and composability for AI agents.

Standard Agent Builder Demo

  • Explanation: Demonstrates building a battery warranty claim agent using Claude Code and the Standard Agent Specification in 5 minutes and 21 seconds.
  • Key claims:
    • Claude Code reads a warranty process PDF and builds a complete standard agent package in minutes.
    • Generated code includes explicit tools, pinned models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), system prompts, threads, and HTTP endpoints.
    • The resulting agent runs in AgentBuilder with full observability into tool calls, token usage, cost, and cache rate.
  • Examples:
    • Building an e-bike battery warranty claim agent for Ottoline using a process PDF.
    • Interacting with the agent via website chat widget backed by both HTTP API and WebSocket API.
  • Terminology:
    • Standard Agent Builder
    • Claude Code
    • Battery warranty agent
    • AgentBuilder admin view
  • Why it matters: Proves that standardized agent specifications enable coding agents to rapidly and reliably build production-ready domain-specific agents.

Key Points

A business is its processes

  • Explanation: All business value—relationships, network effects, and proprietary data—derives from the underlying operational processes.
  • Evidence: Business processes in HVAC repair, universities, and cloud providers dictate organizational success.
  • Practical implication: AI agents must integrate directly into existing business processes rather than acting as generic standalone chatbots.

An agent that can do anything is a liability

  • Explanation: Unconstrained general agents with access to broad toolsets introduce unacceptable risks of unintended actions.
  • Evidence: Grok or Claude with full tool access might check emails or read news instead of completing a warranty claim.
  • Practical implication: Domain-specific agents must have strictly restricted, fine-tuned scopes and workflows.

A Gmail agent beats a Gmail skill

  • Explanation: Specialized single-task agents running on smaller, cheaper models outperform massive general models equipped with dozens of skills.
  • Evidence: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash configured as a dedicated Gmail agent is cheaper, more evaluable, and easier to compose than Claude Opus with 41 skills.
  • Practical implication: Decompose complex systems into hierarchies of small, domain-specific agents.

Everything in the specification is code

  • Explanation: To enable packaging, distribution on npm, and portability, every aspect of an agent must be defined in code.
  • Evidence: TypeScript definitions for models, prompts, tools, handlers, hooks, and effects.
  • Practical implication: Eliminates hand-written prompts and proprietary UI configurations, allowing agents to be shipped on USB sticks or package registries.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Three Factors of Agent Adoption

  • How it works: Evaluates why custom agents are built based on integration depth, trust constraints, and execution efficacy.
  • Components:
    • Integration
    • Trust
    • Efficacy
  • When to use: When designing AI solutions for enterprise business processes.

Standard Agent Specification Architecture

  • How it works: Structures agents as deterministic software harnesses wrapping non-deterministic language models with strict boundaries.
  • Components:
    • Model definition
    • System prompt
    • Tools (Functions, Prompts, Agents)
    • Threads
    • Hooks
    • Effects
    • Endpoints
  • When to use: When building production-grade, multi-agent enterprise systems.

Examples & Case Studies

Grok bot given access to a warranty portal and email inbox checks email and reads election results while attempting to file a claim.

  • Illustrates: The lack of trust and control in general-purpose agents with unconstrained tool access.
  • Lesson: Agents must be strictly limited in scope to ensure they do what they are told and nothing else.

Building an e-bike battery warranty claim agent using Claude Code and a process PDF in 5 minutes and 21 seconds.

  • Illustrates: The speed and consistency enabled by the Standard Agent Specification.
  • Lesson: Coding agents can instantly generate fully compliant, production-ready agent packages when given a standardized spec.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Read the spec at standardagentspec.org
    • Use npx skills add standardagents/skills@standard-agent-spec with your coding agent
  • Strategic:
    • Build domain-specific, packaged, and shared agents rather than massive monolithic prompts
    • Adopt TypeScript and file-based agent definitions for portability and composability
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can non-TypeScript runtimes implement the Standard Agent Specification?
    • What are the best practices for multi-agent hierarchical composition in production?

Claims Worth Verifying

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Justin Schroeder
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Standardizing AI Agents via the Standard Agent Specification
- **Purpose**: To introduce and open-source the Standard Agent Specification and Standard Agent Builder, establishing an open ecosystem of interoperable, domain-specific agents.
Justin Schroeder introduces the Standard Agent Specification, an open-source, engineering-first approach to building, packaging, and running domain-specific AI agents. He highlights why prevailing approaches—such as combining MCP servers and markdown files with general models—fail because businesses require control, reliability, repeatability, and non-generic tone. The talk details the three primary factors for agent adoption (Integration, Trust, Efficacy) and outlines the core specification principles: agents must be vendor-agnostic, domain-specific, coupled to a model, composable, and portable, implemented in TypeScript via file-based definitions, threads, hooks, effects, and runtimes.
## Topic Map
### The Observation: Everyone Is Building Agents
- **Explanation**: An observation that while prevailing wisdom suggests building MCP servers and markdown documentation for smart general models (like Grok or Claude), businesses continue building custom agents because of deeper needs.
- **Key claims**:
  - Everyone is building agents to power their business.
  - Prevailing wisdom says to build MCP servers and markdown files for smart general agents, but companies still build custom agents.
- **Examples**:
  - Grok bot or Claude used with markdown files and MCP servers.
- **Terminology**:
  - MCP servers
  - Agent MD
  - Smart general agent
- **Why it matters**: Highlights the gap between general-purpose AI development and actual enterprise operational requirements.
### The Three Factors: Integration, Trust, Efficacy
- **Explanation**: Explains why people build custom agents based on three primary factors: deep business process integration, strict trust (doing what it was told and nothing else), and efficacy (doing the task well).
- **Key claims**:
  - A business is its processes; everything valuable comes from well-functioning processes.
  - If an agent can do anything, it might do anything, which is an unacceptable liability.
  - Efficacy is about whether an agent can do the task and improve business performance.
- **Examples**:
  - HVAC repair shop managing warranty claims, crew scheduling, and permits.
  - University managing financial aid and admissions.
  - Cloud provider managing incident response and billing disputes.
- **Terminology**:
  - Integration
  - Trust
  - Efficacy
  - Liability
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates why businesses reject unconstrained general agents in favor of tightly scoped, dependable domain-specific workflows.
### The Limits of Current Approaches & The Need for Standards
- **Explanation**: Discusses why single-agent-does-everything approaches and ad-hoc custom harnesses fail to scale, lack distribution, and cannot be easily composed.
- **Key claims**:
  - A Gmail agent beats a Gmail skill because a single-job agent is cheaper, easier to evaluate, and composes into larger systems.
  - Agents are hard because building an agent means building a harness with dozens of complex orchestration requirements.
  - Existing standards cover tool access (MCP), prompts (Skills, Agents.md), and communication (A2A, ACP, payments), but nothing exists for the harness itself.
- **Examples**:
  - Claude Opus 5.5 with 112 tool definitions and 41 skills vs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash running a single-job Gmail agent.
- **Terminology**:
  - The harness
  - MCP
  - Skills
  - A2A
  - ACP
  - Composability
- **Why it matters**: Justifies the necessity of a standardized agent specification rather than fragmented, custom-built harnesses.
### The Standard Agent Specification
- **Explanation**: Introduces the Standard Agent Specification (standardagentspec.org) as an open-source, engineering-first approach where agents are deterministic software harnessing non-deterministic models.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents are deterministic software that harnesses non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective.
  - Five core principles: vendor-agnostic, domain-specific, coupled to a model, composable, and portable.
  - Everything is code written in TypeScript for file-based definitions, typed references, hooks, effects, threads, and runtimes.
- **Examples**:
  - Defining models, prompts, and agents using `defineModel`, `definePrompt`, and `defineAgent` in TypeScript.
- **Terminology**:
  - Standard Agent Specification
  - Deterministic software
  - Vendor-agnostic
  - TypeScript
  - Runtime contract
- **Why it matters**: Provides a concrete engineering specification that solves speed, consistency, portability, and composability for AI agents.
### Standard Agent Builder Demo
- **Explanation**: Demonstrates building a battery warranty claim agent using Claude Code and the Standard Agent Specification in 5 minutes and 21 seconds.
- **Key claims**:
  - Claude Code reads a warranty process PDF and builds a complete standard agent package in minutes.
  - Generated code includes explicit tools, pinned models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), system prompts, threads, and HTTP endpoints.
  - The resulting agent runs in AgentBuilder with full observability into tool calls, token usage, cost, and cache rate.
- **Examples**:
  - Building an e-bike battery warranty claim agent for Ottoline using a process PDF.
  - Interacting with the agent via website chat widget backed by both HTTP API and WebSocket API.
- **Terminology**:
  - Standard Agent Builder
  - Claude Code
  - Battery warranty agent
  - AgentBuilder admin view
- **Why it matters**: Proves that standardized agent specifications enable coding agents to rapidly and reliably build production-ready domain-specific agents.
## Key Points
### A business is its processes
- **Explanation**: All business value—relationships, network effects, and proprietary data—derives from the underlying operational processes.
- **Evidence**: Business processes in HVAC repair, universities, and cloud providers dictate organizational success.
- **Practical implication**: AI agents must integrate directly into existing business processes rather than acting as generic standalone chatbots.
### An agent that can do anything is a liability
- **Explanation**: Unconstrained general agents with access to broad toolsets introduce unacceptable risks of unintended actions.
- **Evidence**: Grok or Claude with full tool access might check emails or read news instead of completing a warranty claim.
- **Practical implication**: Domain-specific agents must have strictly restricted, fine-tuned scopes and workflows.
### A Gmail agent beats a Gmail skill
- **Explanation**: Specialized single-task agents running on smaller, cheaper models outperform massive general models equipped with dozens of skills.
- **Evidence**: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash configured as a dedicated Gmail agent is cheaper, more evaluable, and easier to compose than Claude Opus with 41 skills.
- **Practical implication**: Decompose complex systems into hierarchies of small, domain-specific agents.
### Everything in the specification is code
- **Explanation**: To enable packaging, distribution on npm, and portability, every aspect of an agent must be defined in code.
- **Evidence**: TypeScript definitions for models, prompts, tools, handlers, hooks, and effects.
- **Practical implication**: Eliminates hand-written prompts and proprietary UI configurations, allowing agents to be shipped on USB sticks or package registries.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Three Factors of Agent Adoption
- **How it works**: Evaluates why custom agents are built based on integration depth, trust constraints, and execution efficacy.
- **Components**:
  - Integration
  - Trust
  - Efficacy
- **When to use**: When designing AI solutions for enterprise business processes.
### Standard Agent Specification Architecture
- **How it works**: Structures agents as deterministic software harnesses wrapping non-deterministic language models with strict boundaries.
- **Components**:
  - Model definition
  - System prompt
  - Tools (Functions, Prompts, Agents)
  - Threads
  - Hooks
  - Effects
  - Endpoints
- **When to use**: When building production-grade, multi-agent enterprise systems.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Grok bot given access to a warranty portal and email inbox checks email and reads election results while attempting to file a claim.
- **Illustrates**: The lack of trust and control in general-purpose agents with unconstrained tool access.
- **Lesson**: Agents must be strictly limited in scope to ensure they do what they are told and nothing else.
### Building an e-bike battery warranty claim agent using Claude Code and a process PDF in 5 minutes and 21 seconds.
- **Illustrates**: The speed and consistency enabled by the Standard Agent Specification.
- **Lesson**: Coding agents can instantly generate fully compliant, production-ready agent packages when given a standardized spec.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Read the spec at standardagentspec.org
  - Use `npx skills add standardagents/skills@standard-agent-spec` with your coding agent
- **Strategic**:
  - Build domain-specific, packaged, and shared agents rather than massive monolithic prompts
  - Adopt TypeScript and file-based agent definitions for portability and composability
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can non-TypeScript runtimes implement the Standard Agent Specification?
  - What are the best practices for multi-agent hierarchical composition in production?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Fine-tuning an agent's prompt is more effective than fine-tuning an underlying model. (Technical claim)
- TypeScript is the optimal interpreted language for agent runtimes due to ubiquity and rapid execution. (Architectural opinion)
## Notable Quotes
> "Everyone is building agents." (at 0:10)
> "If an agent can do anything, it might do anything. And that is a liability." (at 7:00)
> "A business is its processes." (at 4:14)
> "Agents are deterministic software that harnesses the non-deterministic results produced by models in pursuit of a desired objective." (at 22:21)
> "Unfortunately, no such spec exists. Until today." (at 21:52)
## Compressed Summary
- Businesses require control, reliability, repeatability, and non-generic tone from AI agents.
- General models with massive toolsets introduce dangerous operational liabilities.
- The Standard Agent Specification provides an open-source, engineering-first framework for TypeScript-based agent definitions.
